ipc.body:
Processes start life as strangers behind locked doors, which keeps a system stable, and yet real work needs them to cooperate, so we need to open a few controlled windows between them. Processes started out as strangers: each has its own address space, so one cannot read or damage another. That isolation is what keeps a system stable, but real work needs cooperation. A compiler pipeline passes text from one stage to the next; a web server hands requests to workers; a database coordinates dozens of clients. The OS therefore offers inter-process communication (IPC), in two basic styles.

With shared memory, the OS maps the same physical page into two address spaces. After the one-time set-up cost, communication is as fast as reading a variable — no kernel call per message — but the processes must now coordinate access themselves, which is the entire subject of this chapter. With message passing, the processes call send and receive and the kernel copies the data. It is slower per message but simple to reason about (the kernel serialises everything) and works unchanged across a network. Pipes (ls | grep), message queues, sockets and signals are all message-passing flavours.

Threads make the problem sharper: they share an address space by default, so every global variable is a shared variable. The rest of this chapter asks one question: when several flows of control touch the same data, how do we keep the data correct?

Name one real program of your own that needs two processes to talk. Would you choose shared memory or message passing for it, and why?
keynotes: Each process has its own address space, so one cannot read or damage another, which keeps the system stable.
Cooperation needs inter-process communication (IPC), in two basic styles: shared memory and message passing.
A compiler pipeline, a web server handing requests to workers and a database serving many clients all need it.

race.body:
Here is the nastiest class of bug in all of programming, one that vanishes when you look for it, and you can understand its root cause with a single line of code. Suppose two processes both run counter++. That single line is really three machine steps: load the counter into a register, add one, store it back. If the scheduler switches between the load and the store, both processes read the same old value and one increment is lost. The final answer depends on the exact interleaving of the two instruction streams — a race condition.

Races are the nastiest class of bug because they are not reproducible. The program is not wrong in any single run; it is wrong sometimes. A test may pass a million times, then fail once on a busy server at 3 a.m. You cannot find a race by thinking about one process alone; you must think about all the ways two instruction streams can interleave. The figure shows the unlucky interleaving: A and B both load 5, both compute 6, both store 6. Two increments, final value 6 instead of 7.

The stretch of code that touches shared data is the critical section. A correct solution to the critical-section problem must satisfy three requirements: mutual exclusion (at most one process inside at a time), progress (if nobody is inside and somebody wants in, the decision cannot be postponed forever and only those who want in take part in it), and bounded waiting (once a process has asked, a limit exists on how many times others may enter before it does — so nobody starves).

Write the three machine steps of counter++ and show an interleaving of two processes where one increment is lost. Why is the bug so hard to reproduce?
keynotes: counter++ is really three machine steps: load the counter into a register, add one, store it back.
If the scheduler switches between the load and the store, both processes read the same old value and one increment is lost.
The result depends on the exact interleaving, a race condition, and races are the nastiest bugs because they are not repeatable.

peterson.body:
Before locks existed, clever people asked whether two processes could keep each other out of a critical section using nothing but ordinary reads and writes, and Peterson found an elegant answer you can follow line by line. Before locks existed, programmers asked whether two processes could achieve mutual exclusion using nothing but ordinary reads and writes of shared variables. Peterson (1981) found an elegant answer. The two processes (0 and 1) share a boolean array flag[2] — “I want to enter” — and an integer turn — “whose turn it is to wait”. To enter, process i executes:

  • flag[i] = true; — announce that I am interested.
  • turn = j; — politely give the other process priority (j = 1 − i).
  • while (flag[j] && turn == j) ; — wait while the other wants in and it is its turn.
  • … critical section …
  • flag[i] = false; — leaving.

Why does it work? Suppose both are in the critical section at once. Then both passed their while test, so each saw either flag[other] == false or turn == itself. But each set its own flag to true before the test, so the loop condition can only have failed because of turn. Both could not have turn equal to themselves — turn holds a single value — which is a contradiction. Progress and bounded waiting follow because a waiting process is released as soon as the other leaves (clearing its flag) or yields the turn.

Peterson’s algorithm is beautiful but not what real systems use. Modern CPUs and compilers reorder memory operations, so without special memory barriers it can fail; and it spins (busy-waits), wasting CPU. Its value is educational: it shows the problem is solvable and what a solution must look like.

Run Peterson’s algorithm by hand for two processes that both want to enter at once. Who goes first, and who politely waits?
keynotes: Peterson (1981) uses a shared boolean array flag[2] (“I want to enter”) and an integer turn (“whose turn it is to wait”).
To enter, process i sets flag[i] = true and turn = j, then waits while flag[j] is true and it is j’s turn.
It gives mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting for two processes using only reads and writes.

hardware.body:
Software solutions are fragile because a read followed by a write is not atomic, and the cure, which you will find on every modern CPU, is to make the pair indivisible. The reason software solutions are fragile is that a read followed by a write is not atomic. The cure is to make the CPU do the pair indivisibly. TestAndSet(lock) returns the old value of a memory word and sets it to 1 in one uninterruptible step; Compare-and-Swap(addr, expected, new) replaces the contents of addr by new only if it currently equals expected, returning whether it did. With test-and-set a lock is one line: while (TestAndSet(&lock)) ; to acquire, lock = 0 to release. Whoever sees the old value 0 gets the lock; everybody else sees 1 and spins.

This spinlock is ideal when the critical section is a handful of instructions and the lock is held on another core for a very short time: spinning costs less than a context switch. It is terrible when the wait is long or on a single core, where spinning merely burns the time the lock-holder needs to finish. Hence the second family of tools: locks that put a waiting process to sleep and wake it when the lock is released.

A last, blunt tool: on a single-CPU kernel the critical section can be protected by disabling interrupts, so no timer interrupt can cause a switch. This is fine inside the kernel for tiny regions, but unacceptable for user programs (a user could hold the CPU forever) and useless on multiprocessors, where another core is unaffected.

Write a spin lock with TestAndSet in one line, then explain why a long wait wastes CPU time. What would you prefer instead?
keynotes: TestAndSet(lock) returns the old value of a memory word and sets it to 1 in one uninterruptible step.
Compare-and-Swap(addr, expected, new) replaces the contents of addr by new only if it currently equals expected.
With test-and-set a lock is one line: while the old value is 1, keep trying.

semaphores.body:
Spinning wastes the processor, so what we want is a lock that lets the waiter go to sleep, and Dijkstra’s semaphore does precisely this. Spinning is wasteful; what we want is a lock that makes the waiter sleep. Dijkstra’s semaphore is exactly that: an integer S with two atomic operations. wait(S) (also called P, from Dutch proberen, “to test”) decrements S; if the result would be negative the caller is placed on the semaphore’s queue and put to sleep. signal(S) (V, verhogen, “to raise”) increments S and, if anyone is sleeping, wakes one. The sign of S tells the story: a positive value is the number of free units, a negative value is minus the number of sleepers.

The initial value defines the use. Initialised to 1 it is a mutex (binary semaphore): wait before the critical section, signal after. Initialised to n it is a counting semaphore guarding n identical resources (a pool of 5 printers). Initialised to 0 it is a signal: one process waits for an event that another announces (“the data is ready”). A mutex proper adds the idea of an owner: only the process that locked it may unlock it.

Semaphores are powerful and easy to get wrong — a forgotten signal deadlocks the system, a swapped pair of wait calls too. A monitor packages the shared data, the operations on it and an implicit lock into one construct (Java synchronized, C# lock), so a caller cannot forget to lock. Inside a monitor, condition variables with wait and signal let a thread sleep until a particular condition holds (“buffer not empty”), releasing the monitor lock while it sleeps.

Explain what the sign of S tells you, and why a semaphore initialised to 1 acts as a mutex while one initialised to 0 is a signal.
keynotes: A semaphore is an integer S with two atomic operations: wait(S) (P) decrements S and sleeps if the result would be negative; signal(S) (V) increments S and wakes one waiter.
The sign of S tells how many resources are free or how many processes are waiting.
A mutex is a semaphore with value 1 plus an owner, and a monitor packages the lock with the data it protects.

classics.body:
Three textbook problems appear in every exam, and each teaches a pattern that you will reuse for the rest of your career. Three textbook problems appear in every exam, and each teaches a pattern. In the bounded buffer (producer–consumer) problem a producer puts items into a buffer of N slots and a consumer takes them out. The producer must wait when the buffer is full, the consumer when it is empty, and they must not touch the buffer at the same instant. Three semaphores solve it: empty = N (free slots), full = 0 (filled slots) and mutex = 1. The producer does wait(empty); wait(mutex); put; signal(mutex); signal(full). The consumer mirrors it with wait(full); wait(mutex); get; signal(mutex); signal(empty). Swapping the two waits in the producer (mutex first) can deadlock: it could hold the mutex while sleeping on empty, and the consumer could never get the mutex to make room.

The readers–writers problem lets many readers share data but gives writers exclusive access. The simple solution (readers never wait unless a writer is inside) can starve writers if readers keep arriving; the opposite policy can starve readers. Choosing who is favoured is the whole design decision.

The dining philosophers are five thinkers around a table with a fork between each pair; each needs both neighbouring forks to eat. If every philosopher picks up the left fork first, all five can hold one fork and wait for the right one forever: a deadlock. Remedies: allow at most four to sit, pick both forks atomically, or break the symmetry (odd philosophers take left first, even take right first). The problem is a model of any process needing two resources.

For the bounded buffer, say which semaphore makes the producer wait when the buffer is full and which makes the consumer wait when it is empty.
keynotes: In the bounded buffer (producer–consumer) problem the producer must wait when the buffer is full, the consumer when it is empty, and they must not touch the buffer together.
Three semaphores solve it: empty = N (free slots), full = 0 (filled slots) and mutex = 1.
The readers–writers and dining philosophers problems teach other patterns.

deadlock.body:
Locks cure races and introduce a new failure, and the picture to keep in mind is two cars meeting on a one-lane bridge with neither able to move. Locks solve races and introduce a new failure. A deadlock is a set of processes each waiting for something only another member of the set can release. The everyday picture is two cars meeting on a one-lane bridge: neither can move until the other backs up. In software, process 1 holds the printer and wants the scanner while process 2 holds the scanner and wants the printer. Nothing is broken, nobody is spinning; they are simply asleep, forever.

Coffman showed that deadlock needs all four of these at once. Mutual exclusion: resources cannot be shared. Hold and wait: a process keeps what it has while asking for more. No pre-emption: resources cannot be forcibly taken away. Circular wait: there is a cycle P1 → P2 → … → P1 of processes each waiting for the next. Break any one and deadlock is impossible. Drawing the situation as a resource-allocation graph makes it visible: processes are circles, resources rectangles, a request is an arrow from process to resource and an assignment an arrow from resource to process. A cycle with single-instance resources is a deadlock; with multiple instances a cycle is necessary but not sufficient.

Check the four conditions against the printer and scanner example: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no pre-emption, circular wait. Which one would you break?
keynotes: A deadlock is a set of processes each waiting for something only another member of the set can release.
Process 1 holds the printer and wants the scanner while process 2 holds the scanner and wants the printer.
Four conditions must hold together: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no pre-emption and circular wait.

handling.body:
Four strategies exist for dealing with deadlock, and exam answers should name all four, so let’s see what each of them costs you. Four strategies exist, and exam answers should name all four. Ignore it (the ostrich algorithm): if deadlocks are rare and the cost of preventing them is high, do nothing and let the user reboot — what Unix and Windows effectively do for application-level deadlocks. Prevention breaks one of the four conditions by design: spool output (removes exclusion), require all resources at once or release before asking (breaks hold-and-wait), allow pre-emption of memory and CPU (breaks no-pre-emption), impose a global resource ordering (breaks circular wait). It works but can waste resources and reduce concurrency.

Avoidance allows all four conditions but looks at each request and refuses it if it could lead to a deadlock; it needs advance knowledge of each process’s maximum claim and is embodied in the banker’s algorithm, next. Detection and recovery lets deadlocks occur, runs an algorithm periodically (a cycle search in the wait-for graph, or a banker-like check for multiple instances) and then recovers by killing processes one at a time or all at once, or by pre-empting resources and rolling a victim back to a checkpoint. Choosing the victim by priority, work done and resources held is itself a policy decision, and starvation of the same victim must be avoided.

Match each strategy to a real system: the ostrich algorithm, prevention, avoidance and detection. Which would you use for a hospital machine, and which for a laptop?
keynotes: Ignore it (the ostrich algorithm): if deadlocks are rare and prevention is costly, do nothing and let the user reboot.
Prevention breaks one of the four conditions by design, for example by spooling output or requiring all resources at once.
Avoidance (the banker’s algorithm) and detection with recovery are the other two.

banker.body:
Think of a banker who only lends if he can still guarantee that everyone will eventually be able to borrow up to their limit and repay, and you have the whole idea of the algorithm. The banker treats each process's maximum claim like a credit line. A bank with limited cash lends to customers only if it can still guarantee that every customer will eventually be able to borrow up to their limit, finish their business and repay. The OS does the same: before granting a request it asks, “after this grant, can everybody still finish?” A state is safe if there is some order in which every process can be given its remaining need and finish. An unsafe state is not a deadlock — it is a state from which deadlock can no longer be ruled out.

The data are four: Available (a vector of free units of each resource), Max (each process’s declared maximum), Allocation (what each holds now) and Need = Max − Allocation. The safety algorithm sets Work = Available and repeatedly looks for an unfinished process whose Need fits inside Work; it pretends that process runs to completion and adds its Allocation back to Work. If all processes can be retired this way, the state is safe and the order found is a safe sequence; if it gets stuck with some processes unfinished, the state is unsafe.

To handle a request from process i, check it does not exceed Need[i], and does not exceed Available (else i must wait). Then pretend to grant it — subtract from Available, add to Allocation[i], subtract from Need[i] — and run the safety algorithm. Safe: grant it for real. Unsafe: undo the pretence and make i wait. Run the classic example: 5 processes, 3 resource types, Available = (3 3 2); then the request card, where P1 asks for (1 0 2).

Take a small table of Allocation, Max and Available and look for an order in which every process can finish. If there is one, the state is safe.
keynotes: The banker treats each process’s maximum claim like a credit line.
Before granting a request the OS asks, “after this grant, can everybody still finish?”
A state is safe if there is some order in which every process can be given its maximum and finish.

detect.body:
If you decide not to prevent deadlock you must find it afterwards, and the question of how reduces to finding a loop in a picture of who waits for whom. When resources have a single instance each, detection reduces to finding a cycle in a wait-for graph (an arrow P→Q means “P waits for a resource held by Q”); a depth-first search finds one in O(n²) or O(n + e). For several instances per resource the banker-like detection algorithm is used: it marks processes whose current request (not worst-case need) can be satisfied, and any process left unmarked is deadlocked. Detection costs CPU, so systems run it only when CPU utilisation falls or every few minutes.

The best defence in application code is simple: keep critical sections short; never call unknown code while holding a lock; acquire multiple locks in one global order; prefer try-lock with timeout over waiting forever; and use higher-level structures (queues, thread pools) so less hand-written locking is needed. Databases add timeouts and rollback: a transaction that waits too long is aborted and retried — recovery by victim selection.

Draw a wait-for graph of three processes with a cycle and one without. Which has a deadlock, and which process would you abort to break it?
keynotes: With one instance per resource, detection finds a cycle in a wait-for graph (P→Q means P waits for a resource held by Q).
A depth-first search finds one in O(n²) or O(n + e).
For several instances a banker-like algorithm marks processes whose current request can be satisfied, and any process left unmarked is deadlocked.

practice.body:
Now you try, because this chapter is learned by doing.

After each numerical, explain your answer aloud as if teaching a friend.
keynotes: Work each numerical on paper before opening the answer.
For the banker’s algorithm, compute Need = Max − Allocation and look for a safe order.
Check deadlock numericals by drawing the wait-for graph.

summary.body:
Here is what to remember from the chapter, in a handful of lines you can revise from.

  • A race condition is a bug in the interleaving, not in any one process; a critical section guarded by a lock removes it. A correct solution gives mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.
  • Peterson’s algorithm solves it for two processes with reads and writes alone; real systems use atomic instructions (test-and-set, compare-and-swap) and sleeping locks.
  • Mutex = semaphore with value 1 plus an owner; semaphore 0 = signalling; semaphore n = pool. Order of waits matters (counting semaphore first, mutex second).
  • Deadlock needs all four conditions; breaking one prevents it. Systems choose between ignoring, preventing, avoiding (banker) and detecting-and-recovering.
  • Safe ⇒ no deadlock guaranteed; unsafe ⇒ deadlock possible. The banker only ever grants requests that keep the state safe.

Cover the bullets and recite the three requirements of a correct solution to the critical-section problem. Then check yourself.
keynotes: A race condition is a bug in the interleaving, and a critical section guarded by a lock removes it.
A correct solution gives mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting; real systems use atomic instructions and sleeping locks.
A mutex is a semaphore with value 1 plus an owner, and semaphore 0 is for signalling.
